title: The Interview
blurb: The job you need is one interview away — at two o'clock today. But the trains are down, a document is missing, and a smooth stranger is offering an easy way to fake your way in. With the clock running and someone from your past on the panel, you have one morning to get there as yourself — and earn it honestly.

identity.name: Interview at Two
identity.mood: A cold morning, a warm chance: the interview that could change everything is at two, and the city is against you.

cover.alt: A warm-lit interview-room window high in a cool glass tower at dusk, rain on the street below, one warm window among the cold ones.

line.en: The interview that could change everything is at two o'clock, and the morning is already against you. Get there, as yourself, and earn it straight.
line.fr: L'entretien qui peut tout changer est à quatorze heures, et la matinée est déjà contre toi. Arrives-y en restant toi-même, et mérite-le honnêtement.
line.es: La entrevista que podría cambiarlo todo es a las dos, y la mañana ya está en tu contra. Llega allí siendo tú mismo, y gánatelo con honradez.
line.it: Il colloquio che potrebbe cambiare tutto è alle due, e la mattinata è già contro di te. Arrivaci restando te stesso, e meritatelo con onestà.
line.de: Das Vorstellungsgespräch, das alles verändern könnte, ist um zwei, und der Morgen ist schon gegen dich. Komm hin, bleib du selbst, und verdien es dir ehrlich.
line.pt: A entrevista que pode mudar tudo é às duas, e a manhã já está contra ti. Chega lá sendo tu mesmo, e merece-a com honestidade.
line.ru: Собеседование, которое может изменить всё, — в два часа, а утро уже против тебя. Доберись туда, оставаясь собой, и заслужи это честно.
line.zh: 那场可能改变一切的面试在两点，而这个上午已经处处跟你作对。赶到那里，做你自己，堂堂正正地赢下它。
line.ar: المقابلة التي قد تُغيّر كل شيء في الساعة الثانية، والصباح بالفعل ضدّك. اوصل إلى هناك كما أنت، واستحقّها بنزاهة.

hero.sub: A story where you are the hero — and every choice turns you to a new page. Written for people learning English, at your level, with meaning in your language whenever you need it.

text.A2: It is one o'clock. The interview that could change everything is at two. You have been out of work for months. The rent is late, and your dad is counting on you. But your bag is a mess, one paper is missing, and the trains are down. Getting there is all on you now.
text.B1: It is one o'clock, and the interview that could change everything is at two. You have been out of work for months now. The rent is late, and your dad is counting on you. But your bag is a mess, the one paper you need is missing, and the trains are down. For the first time, getting there is all on you.
text.B2: It is one o'clock, and the interview that could change everything is at two. You have been out of work for months now, and it shows. The rent is late, and your dad — who always said you'd land on your feet — is counting on you. But your bag is a mess, the one paper you really need is missing, and the trains are down across the city. For the first time, getting there, as yourself and on time, is all on you.

text.A2: Take stock of what you have.
text.B1: Take stock of what you have.
text.B2: Take stock of what you have.

text.A2: You look at what you have to work with. Your one good suit, the job advert, a pen, your phone. But the paper with the address and the time is gone. It is already past one, and the clock is loud in your head. You must decide what to do, and move fast.
text.B1: You look at what you have to work with. Your one good suit, the job advert, a pen, your phone. But the paper with the address and the time on it is gone. It's already past one, and the clock is loud in your head. You have to decide what to do, and move fast.
text.B2: You look at what you have to work with. Your one good suit, the printed job advert, a pen that still works, your phone. But the paper with the address and the time on it — the one thing you can't do without — is gone. It's already past one, and the clock is loud in your head. You have to decide what to do, and you have to move fast.

text.A2: You call an old workmate to ask what to do. The phone rings and rings. Then she picks up. She can't meet you — she's miles away. But she talks you through it, calmly. 'Be yourself,' she says. 'You've done the work. You can do this.' And somehow you start to believe her.
text.B1: You call an old workmate to ask what to do. The phone rings and rings, and then at last she picks up. She can't meet you — she's miles away. But she talks you through it, calmly, step by step. 'Be yourself,' she says. 'You've done the work. You can do this.' And somehow you start to believe her.
text.B2: You call an old workmate to ask what on earth to do. The phone rings and rings, and then at last she picks up. She can't meet you today — she's miles away across the country. But she talks you through it anyway, calmly, step by step. 'Be yourself,' she says. 'You've done the work. You can do this.' And somehow, hearing her, you start to believe it.

text.A2: You call home first. Your dad picks up, and his voice steadies you at once. 'You'll be grand,' he says. But the clock is still running, and you are still not ready. Sitting on the phone won't get you there. You need your papers, a plan, and a clear head before you go.
text.B1: You call home first. Your dad picks up, and his voice steadies you at once. 'You'll be grand,' he says. But the clock is still running, and you're still not ready. Sitting on the phone won't get you there. You need your papers, a plan, and a clear head before you go.
text.B2: You call home first, before anything else. Your dad picks up, and his voice steadies you at once. 'You'll be grand,' he says, the way he always does. But the clock is still running, and you're still not ready. Sitting on the phone to him won't get you across the city. You need your papers, a plan, and a clear head before you so much as leave the flat.

text.A2: You pull yourself together and get ready. You press your shirt, check your shoes, and breathe. Outside, the street is grey and wet. Then your phone buzzes — a message from a number you don't know. 'I can help you get that job,' it says. You weren't expecting anything like that.
text.B1: You pull yourself together and get ready to go. You press your shirt, check your shoes, and breathe. Outside, the street is grey and wet. Then your phone buzzes — a message from a number you don't know. 'I can help you get that job,' it says. You weren't expecting anything like that, not today.
text.B2: You pull yourself together and get ready to go. You press your shirt, check your shoes, and try to breathe slowly. Outside, the street is grey and wet and unhelpful. Then your phone buzzes — a message from a number you don't recognise. 'I can help you get that job,' it says, and nothing more. You weren't expecting anything like that, not today of all days.

text.A2: You make yourself stop and think. You could set off right now and sort the rest on the way. You could get your papers in order first. Or you could call round for help and a lift. Each choice costs time you don't have. And the clock keeps moving toward two.
text.B1: You make yourself stop and think. You could set off right now and sort the rest on the way. You could get your papers in order first. Or you could call round for help and a lift. Each choice costs time you don't have — and the clock keeps moving toward two.
text.B2: You make yourself stop and think for a moment. You could set off right now and sort the rest out on the way. You could get all your papers in order first, properly. Or you could call round for help and maybe a lift across town. Each choice costs time you don't have — and the clock keeps moving, steadily, toward two.

text.A2: The time presses on you like a weight. You think of the panel waiting at two, of the late rent, of your dad's quiet hope. A whole new life rests on this one hour. That isn't a worry; it's a plain fact. No one else can walk in there for you. It is you, today, or no one.

text.A2: The print shop is still open. Old Sam waves you in out of the rain. 'Use the machine,' he says. 'Pay me when you can.' He points you to it. Print your CV, your letter, the address, the map. Everything you need to walk in ready. He's a good sort, Sam.
text.B1: The print shop is still open, and old Sam waves you in out of the rain. 'Use the machine,' he says. 'Pay me when you can.' He points you to it. Print your CV, your letter, the address, the map. Everything you need to walk in ready is here. He's a good sort, Sam.
text.B2: The print shop is still open, and old Sam waves you in out of the rain. 'Use the machine,' he says. 'Pay me when you're able.' He points you to it in the corner. Print your CV, your covering letter, the address, the map — everything you need to walk in ready is right here. He's a good sort, Sam, and always has been.

text.A2: Near the station, you see her. A young woman stands frozen at the barrier, her ticket jammed, the crowd pushing past. She can't get through, and no one stops. 'Can you help?' she asks. You've an interview to reach and no time. But she's right here, stuck, and asking you.

text.B2: Near the station, you see her. A young woman stands frozen at the ticket barrier, her ticket jammed, the crowd pushing past on both sides. She can't get through, and no one stops for her. text.A2: You just set off, fast and half-ready. You grab your bag and go. But you've no real plan, and half your papers are loose in your hand. Rushing like this, it won't come together on its own. You can't just turn up and hope for the best.

text.A2: You make your calls, asking the same thing each time. Can you help me get there? Send me the address. Give me a lift. Steady my nerves. Some say no — too busy, too far, bad timing. But a few say yes, and come through. Today, a few is enough.
text.B1: You make your calls, asking the same thing each time. Can you help me get there? Send me the address. Give me a lift. Steady my nerves. Some say no — too busy, too far, bad timing. But a few say yes, and come through for you. Today, a few is more than enough.
text.B2: You make your calls, asking the same thing each time. Can you help me get there? Send me the address. Give me a lift across town. Steady my nerves. Some say no — too busy, too far, bad timing all round. But a few say yes, and come through for you at once. Today, a few willing people is more than enough.

text.A2: You take charge of yourself and your papers. You lay it all out: your CV, the advert, your notes, the address. Done well, this is a real shot at the job. Rushed or half-done, and you walk in with nothing. So you take a breath and get it right, carefully.

text.B2: You take charge of yourself and your papers. You lay it all out neatly on the table: your CV, the printed advert, your notes, the address. So you take a slow breath and get it right, carefully, one thing at a time.

text.A2: You grab just the essentials — your CV and your phone — and go. It feels good to be moving at last. But it isn't a plan, and you've left things behind. You'll still need the rest, and soon. If not, you'll stand in that room with empty hands.

text.B2: You grab just the bare essentials — your CV and your phone — and go. It feels good to be moving at last, after all the panic. But it isn't a plan, and you've left real things behind. You'll still need the rest, and soon. If you don't go back for them, you'll be standing in that room with empty hands and nothing to show.

text.A2: Old Frank trained you years back, and he's seen it all. 'Don't cut the line to save time,' he says. 'It's not worth it — they always see.' He warns you about Reese too, the fixer. 'Walk in as yourself. Answer straight, stay calm. That's the whole job today.'
text.B1: Old Frank trained you years back, and he's seen it all in his time. 'Don't cut the line to save ten minutes,' he says. 'It's not worth it — they always see.' He warns you about Reese too, the fixer. 'Walk in as yourself. Answer straight, stay calm. That's the whole job today.'
text.B2: Old Frank trained you years back, and he's seen it all in his long time. 'Don't ever cut the line to save ten minutes,' he says. 'It's not worth it — they always see, in the end.' He warns you about Reese too, the fixer who works the station. 'Walk in as yourself. Answer straight, stay calm, and don't pretend. That's the whole job today.'

text.A2: You stop and help the stranger. He's an older man who's dropped his bag and papers all over the wet path. You gather them up and walk him to a dry seat. Little by little he calms down. 'Thank you,' he says, gripping your hand. You point him on his way, then turn back to the clock.

text.A2: Getting there comes first. The rest can wait a moment. But you still have to choose how. You could stop at the print shop for what you need first. Or you could set off now and sort the rest as you go.

text.A2: The rush catches up with you. Your hands shake, your heart races, and the clock won't stop. You're trying to do too much at once, and you know it. If you lose your head now, you'll lose the room. So slow down, breathe, one thing at a time.

text.A2: You call round, and people come through. One texts you the address. One offers a lift. One sends a kind word to steady your nerves. Bit by bit, you're not so alone. You still walk in by yourself. But now the getting-there isn't all on you — and that changes things.

text.A2: No one can help. One is at work, one is far away, one just doesn't pick up. You can't make them. So you square your shoulders and go on alone. It's harder this way. But the interview is at two, ready or not.

text.A2: You're on your way across the city. To reach the office in time, you have to cross town. There are two ways. The long way round is safe but slow. Cutting through and jumping the queue is quick. But it's risky, and people are watching.

text.A2: You take old Frank's words to heart. Walk in as yourself. Answer straight. Don't trust Reese. And don't cut any corners. It's simple advice, and good. Now you just have to follow it, with the clock running down.

text.A2: You feel better for the good turn you did. Helping someone, oddly, seems to steady you too. Your head is clearer, your hands are surer. There's still a lot to face before two. But now you feel able to meet it.

text.A2: In the waiting room, the other candidates sit stiff and silent. You break the ice — a small joke, a shared nerve. Slowly the room loosens up. 'You go next,' someone says, and you help each other get ready. It's a good feeling, with the clock running down.

text.A2: The long way is cold and wet, the rain on your face, no shelter at all. But it's safe, and it gets you there. So you keep walking, as fast as you dare, step after step. The clock ticks, but your feet keep moving.

text.A2: Jumping the queue up front would save you twenty minutes, and the platform is right there. But the guards are watching, the crowd is tight, and getting caught means losing it all. Frank told you not to cut the line. And he wasn't joking.

text.A2: You push into the front of the queue, past everyone waiting. At once it feels wrong. People glare and mutter, and a guard turns his head. Every step forward is a gamble now. And there's no going back once you've jumped the line.

text.B2: You help the young woman up and gather her scattered things. Her eyes fill with relief. She presses a small card into your hand — a name at the very firm you're headed to. 'Ask for her,' she says. 'Tell her I sent you.' A small thing — but freely given, in the rain, and you take it and go on your way.

text.A2: You can't stop now — but you can't just leave her, either. So you promise to send help soon. 'Hang on,' you say. 'Stay here, stay dry — someone will come.' You mean it, too. And then you turn and go.
text.B1: You can't stop now — but you can't just leave her, either. So you promise to send help soon. 'Hang on,' you say. 'Stay here, stay dry — someone will come for you.' You mean it, too. And then you turn and go.
text.B2: You can't stop now — but you can't simply leave her there, either. So you promise to send help soon. 'Hang on,' you say, over the rain. 'Stay here, stay dry — someone will come for you.' You mean it, too; and then you turn and go, carrying the weight of it with you.

text.A2: You get one good thing going — you help calm the whole waiting room at once. People breathe easier. Someone shares water, someone shares a laugh. It isn't the interview itself. But it's real, and it's a start.
text.B1: You get one good thing going — you help calm the whole waiting room at once. People breathe easier around you. Someone shares water, someone shares a laugh. It isn't the interview itself. But it's real, and it's a good start.
text.B2: You get one good thing going — you help calm the whole tense waiting room at once. People breathe easier around you now. Someone shares a bottle of water, someone shares a nervous laugh. It isn't the interview itself, not by a long way. But it's real, and it's a good start, and the room feels warmer for it.

text.A2: Person by person, the panic turns into a calm room. People have focus now: one reads notes, one breathes slow, one cheers the next in. Worry turns into doing. And doing beats worrying, every time. The room fills with a quiet, steady warmth.
text.B1: Person by person, the panic turns into a calm room. People have focus now: one reads notes, one breathes slow, one cheers the next one in. Worry turns into doing. And doing beats worrying, every single time. The room fills with a quiet, steady warmth.
text.B2: Person by person, nerve by nerve, the panic turns into a calm room. People have focus now: one reads over notes, one breathes slow, one quietly cheers the next one in. Worry turns into doing — and doing beats worrying, in a waiting room, every single time. The room fills with a quiet, steady warmth, and the worst of the fear lifts.

text.A2: The long morning wears at you. A voice says: give up, go home, tell them you were ill. No one would blame you, and it would be easy. But you think of your dad's face, and the room at two. And you push the voice away. Not yet.
text.B1: The long morning wears at you. A small voice says: give up, go home, tell them you were ill — no one would blame you, and it would be so easy. But you think of your dad's face, and the room at two. And you push the voice away. Not yet. Not while it can still go right.
text.B2: The long morning wears at you. A small voice says: give up, go home, tell them you were ill — no one would blame you, and it would be so easy to do. But you think of your dad's face, and the room waiting at two. And you push the voice away. Not yet. Not while this can still go right.

text.A2: You duck under a café awning to read your notes again. Half the ink has run in the rain. You could push on and trust what you remember. Or something makes you look up — and across the street, a face you half know.
text.B1: You duck under a café awning to read your notes again. Half the ink has run in the rain. You could push on and trust what you remember. Or something makes you look up — and there, across the street, a face you half know.
text.B2: You duck under a café awning to read your notes one more time. Half the ink has run and smudged in the rain. You could push on and trust what you remember. Or something makes you look up — and there, across the wet street, a face you half know, half dread.

text.A2: Reese leans in close, all friendly. 'Rough day,' he says. 'I've got it all — the questions, a reference, a name on the panel. Learn the lines and walk in, no one any the wiser. Why put yourself through this?' His smile is wide. But his eyes don't smile with it.
text.B1: Reese leans in close, all friendly. 'Rough day,' he says. 'I've got it all — the questions, a reference, a name on the panel. Learn the lines and walk in, and no one's any the wiser. Why put yourself through this?' His smile is wide. But his eyes don't smile with it.
text.B2: Reese leans in close, all friendly. 'Rough day,' he says. 'I've got it all — the questions in advance, a glowing reference, a friendly name on the panel. Learn the lines and walk in, and no one's ever any the wiser. Why put yourself through all this?' His smile is wide and easy. But his eyes don't smile along with it, and you notice that.

text.A2: 'Fair price,' Reese says, and names a sum that makes you blink. It's a lot. But he's quick, he's sure, and he's right here. No sweat, no nerves, no risk of a blank. So: pay him, turn him down, or ask him straight what his game is?
text.B1: 'Fair price,' Reese says, and names a sum that makes you blink. It's a lot of money. But he's quick, he's sure, and he's right here in front of you. No sweat, no nerves, no risk of a blank. So what's it to be — pay him, turn him down, or ask what his game is?
text.B2: 'Fair price,' Reese says, and names a sum that makes you blink in the rain. It's a lot of money, more than you've got spare. But he's quick, he's sure of himself, and he's right here in front of you now. No sweat, no nerves, no risk of a blank in the room. So what's it to be — pay him, turn him down flat, or ask him straight out what his game really is?

text.A2: You say no thanks and walk on. It feels good to turn him down. He calls after you, but you don't look back. His sort always find someone. But it won't be you, not today.
text.B1: You say no thanks and walk on past him. It feels good to turn him down. He calls something after you, but you don't look back. His sort always find someone, in the end. But it won't be you, not today.
text.B2: You say no thanks and walk on past him into the rain. It feels good to turn him down flat. He calls something after you, but you don't look back. His sort always find someone, in the end — someone tired and frightened enough. But it won't be you, not today.

text.A2: You take his papers and hand over the money. Your hand closes on the envelope, and part of you already knows. His smile grows. 'Smart move,' he says. But it doesn't feel smart. It feels like a small lie starting.
text.B1: You take his papers and hand over the money. Your hand closes on the envelope, and part of you already knows. His smile grows. 'Smart move,' he says. But it doesn't feel smart at all. It feels like a small lie, just starting.
text.B2: You take his papers and hand over the money. Your hand closes on the envelope, and part of you already knows the truth of it. His smile grows. 'Smart move,' he says. But it doesn't feel smart at all. It feels, in the cold, like a small lie being told — one you'll have to keep telling in that room.

text.A2: You ask him straight: why so keen to help? He laughs. 'Easy money, friend,' he says. 'Flop today, and you'll be back to me next time.' He's honest, at least. That tells you all you need to know.
text.B1: You ask him straight: why is he so keen to help? He laughs. 'Easy money, friend,' he says. 'Flop today, and you'll be back to me next time.' He laughs again. At least he's honest — and that tells you all you need to know.
text.B2: You ask him straight out: why is he so keen to help? He laughs, quite openly. 'Easy money, friend,' he says. 'Flop today, and you'll be back to me next time, won't you.' He laughs again. At least he's honest — and that, right there, tells you everything you need to know.

text.A2: You try to learn his lines on the way. But up close they're all wrong — stiff, false, nothing like you. They won't hold up for a second across that table. The whole thing already feels like a mistake.
text.B1: You try to learn his lines on the way. But up close they're all wrong — stiff, false, nothing like the way you talk. They won't hold up for a second across that table. The whole thing already feels like a mistake.
text.B2: You try to learn his lines on the way there. But up close they're all wrong — stiff, false, nothing at all like the way you actually talk. They won't hold up for a second across that table, under real questions. And the whole thing already feels, in your stomach, like a mistake.

text.A2: You open the envelope, and your heart sinks. A half-real reference, a name spelled wrong, answers to the wrong job. This won't pass in the room for a minute. You paid good money, and it's worthless. The bad feeling in your gut was right.
text.B1: You open the envelope, and your heart sinks — a half-real reference, a name spelled wrong, answers to the wrong job. This won't pass in the room for a minute. You paid good money for it, and it's worthless. The bad feeling in your gut was right all along.
text.B2: You open the envelope, and your heart sinks right through the floor — a half-real reference, a name spelled wrong, answers to the wrong job entirely. This won't pass in that room for a single minute. You paid good money for it, out here in the rain, and it's worthless. The bad feeling in your gut was right about him all along.

text.A2: You turn to find Reese, but he's already gone, off into the crowd. He was never really helping. He just wanted the sale, and you flustered so you'd come back. You've been had, plain and simple.
text.B1: You turn to find Reese, but he's already gone, off into the crowd. He was never really helping you. He just wanted the sale — and you flustered, so you'd come back to him. You've been had, plain and simple.
text.B2: You turn to find Reese, but he's already gone, melted off into the crowd. He was never really helping you at all. He just wanted the sale — and you flustered and shaken, so you'd be back to him next time. You've been had, out here, plain and simple. The rain keeps on, and the money's gone with him.

text.A2: He's gone, and the street is empty. Just the rain now, and the money you gave him for nothing. You learned something today. And you paid too much for it. Now you go on with less than you had.
text.B1: He's gone, and the street is empty — just the rain now, and the money you handed him for nothing. You learned something today. And you paid far too much for it. Now you go on with less than you started with.
text.B2: He's gone, and the street is empty — just the rain now, the cold, and the money you handed him for nothing at all. You learned something today, out here. And you paid far too much for it. Now you go on with less than you started with, and the clock no kinder.

text.A2: Stand a moment in the rain.
text.B1: Stand a moment in the rain.
text.B2: Stand a moment in the rain.

text.A2: Other nervous people are paying Reese too, cash in hand, glad of the easy way. He takes it slow, with that same smile. He only helps the ones who pay the most.
text.B1: Other nervous people are paying Reese too — cash in hand, glad of the easy way out. He takes it slow, with that same smile. He only ever helps the ones who can pay the most.
text.B2: Other nervous people are paying Reese too — cash in hand, glad of any easy way out today. He takes it slow, unhurried, with that same wide smile. He only ever helps the ones who can pay him the most — and you see the whole of him in it. And you want no part of it.

text.A2: You're halfway through the crush now, past most of the queue. The gate looks close — or does it? The crowd and the noise play tricks. And you're a long way from where you should be.
text.B1: You're halfway through the crush now, past most of the queue. The gate looks close — or does it? The crowd and the noise play tricks on you. And you're a long way from where you should be.
text.B2: You're halfway through the crush now, shoved past most of the queue. The gate looks close — or does it? The crowd and the noise and the shouting play tricks on your nerves. And you're a long way from where you should be, out of line, exposed. You keep your eyes down and your feet moving.

text.A2: A guard steps out of the crowd, straight at you, his hand up. This is the moment. You can push on and hope he lets it go. Or you can step back into the line, while you still can.
text.B1: A guard steps out of the crowd, straight at you, his hand up. This is the moment. You can push on and hope he lets it go. Or you can step back into the line, while you still can.
text.B2: A guard steps out of the crowd, straight at you, his hand raised. This is the moment, and it's a short one. You can push on and hope he lets it go. Or you can step back into the line, right now, while you still can. There is no third way out of this one.

text.A2: You get through at last, heart going hard — but through. Somehow you made it. Now you must choose. Push on, rattled as you are? Or go back for the bag you dropped in the crush?
text.B1: You get through at last, heart going hard — but through. Somehow you made it. Now you have to decide: push on, rattled as you are, or go back for the bag you dropped in the crush.
text.B2: You get through at last, your heart going hard against your ribs — but through. Somehow, against the odds, you made it. Now you have to decide: push on, rattled as you are, or go back for the bag you dropped in the crush behind you. Either way, the clock will not wait for you.

text.A2: You step back into the line just in time — the hard, right choice. The guard's eyes move on past you. You stand there, heart racing, but safe. The day isn't lost. But you've lost time you'll miss, and you'll go the long way now.
text.B1: You step back into the line just in time — the hard, right choice. The guard's eyes move on past you. You stand there, heart racing, but safe. The day isn't lost. But you've lost time you'll miss — and you'll go the long way now.
text.B2: You step back into the line just in time — the hard choice, and the right one. The guard's eyes move on past you, and away. You stand there, heart racing, but safe. The day isn't lost. But you've lost time you'll badly miss — and you'll go the long way round now, like you should have.

text.A2: You try to help the lad calm down — slow his breathing, run through a question, find his feet. It helps a little. But he's got next to nothing ready, and you can't stay long. There's really only one thing you can do for him.
text.B1: You try to help the lad calm down — slow his breathing, run through a question, find his feet. It helps a little. But he's got next to nothing ready, and you can't stay long. There's really only one thing you can do for him.
text.B2: You try to help the lad calm down — slow his breathing, run through a question or two, help him find his feet again. It helps a little. But he's got next to nothing ready, and you can't stay long today. There's really only one thing left that you can do for him.

text.A2: You hand him your own notes, and his face changes. He grips them like a lifeline. The grey goes out of his cheeks. 'Thank you,' he says — then he tells you someone's been asking for you, up ahead.
text.B1: You hand him your own notes, and his face changes. He grips them like a lifeline. The grey goes out of his cheeks. 'Thank you,' he says — and then he tells you that someone's been asking for you, up ahead.
text.B2: You hand him your own notes, and his tired face changes all at once. He grips them like a lifeline. The grey goes out of his cheeks. 'Thank you,' he says, over and over — and then he tells you that someone's been asking for you, up ahead, by name.

text.A2: With your notes given away, your heart sinks a little. Now there's less in your own hand for the room. You gave it to help, and you'd do it again. But the clock doesn't care about that. It just keeps ticking.
text.B1: With your notes given away, your heart sinks a little. Now there's less in your own hand for the room. You gave it to help, and you'd do it again. But the clock doesn't care about any of that. It just keeps ticking on.
text.B2: With your notes given away, your heart sinks a little in your chest. Now there's that much less in your own hand for the room at two. You gave it away to help, and you'd do it again in a heartbeat. But the clock doesn't care about any of that. It just keeps ticking on toward the hour.

text.A2: Someone waves you into a warm café. 'Just five minutes,' they say. 'Sit down, dry off, have a cuppa.' It's warm in there. Your nerves beg you to stop. But five minutes can turn into twenty.
text.B1: Someone waves you into a warm café. 'Just five minutes,' they say. 'Sit down, dry off, have a cuppa.' It's warm and dry inside, and your frayed nerves beg you to stop. But five minutes like this can quietly turn into twenty.
text.B2: Someone waves you into a warm, bright café out of the rain. 'Just five minutes,' they say. 'Sit down, dry off, have a cuppa.' It's warm and dry in there, and your frayed nerves beg you to stop a while. But five minutes like this one can quietly turn into twenty, with the clock running.

text.A2: You press on through the rain, cold and wet. Your bag is heavy, the clock in your head. Each step is a small effort now. But you keep them coming, one after another, toward the office and the room.
text.B1: You press on through the rain, cold and wet, your bag heavy, the clock ticking in your head. Each step is a small effort now. But you keep them coming, one after another, toward the office and the room.
text.B2: You press on through the rain, cold and wet to the skin, your bag heavy in your hand and the clock ticking loud in your head. Each step is a small effort on its own now. But you keep them coming, one after another after another, toward the office and the waiting room.

text.A2: An usher stops you. 'There's someone over there,' she says, 'having a bad turn, gone to pieces. No one is helping.' Across the busy hall, a person stands shaking, eyes shut. If no one goes to them, they'll be stuck like that a long while.
text.B1: An usher stops you. 'There's someone over there,' she says, 'having a bad turn, gone to pieces. No one's helping.' Across the busy hall, a person stands shaking, eyes shut tight. If no one goes to them, they'll be stuck like that a long while.
text.B2: An usher stops you in the hall. 'There's someone over there,' she says, 'having a bad turn, gone quite to pieces. No one's helping.' Across the busy concourse, a person stands shaking, eyes shut tight against it all. If no one goes to them now, they'll be stuck like that a long while.

text.A2: You find them by the wall, shaking and lost, too far gone to speak. The panic has them tight. They don't seem to know where they are. You take a firm hold of their arm. 'Breathe with me,' you say. 'You're all right now. I've got you.'
text.B1: You find them by the wall, shaking and lost, too far gone to speak. The panic has them tight. They don't seem to know quite where they are. You take a firm hold of their arm. 'Breathe with me,' you say. 'You're all right now. I've got you.'
text.B2: You find them by the wall, shaking and lost, too far gone to speak. The panic has them tight in its grip. They don't seem to know quite where they are, or who you are. You take a firm hold of their arm. 'Breathe with me,' you say, low and steady. 'You're all right now. I've got you.'

text.A2: You can't do it all at once, and the room needs you most. So you find a guard and send help their way, and press on. It sits badly with you. But today you have to choose, and keep on choosing.
text.B1: You can't do it all at once, and the room needs you most of all. So you find a guard and send help their way, and press on. It sits badly with you. But today you have to choose, and keep on choosing.
text.B2: You can't do it all at once, and the room needs you most of all today. So you find a guard and send help their way, and press on through the hall. It sits badly with you, and will for a while. But today you have to choose, and keep on choosing.

text.A2: You walk them safely to the first-aid desk, where staff take over. Their face fills with relief. Someone brings water and a chair. 'Thank you,' they keep saying to you. But your own room is waiting, and you can't stay long today.
text.B1: You walk them safely to the first-aid desk, where the staff take over. Their face fills with relief. Someone brings water and a chair. 'Thank you,' they keep saying to you. But your own room is waiting, and you can't stay long today.
text.B2: You walk them safely across to the first-aid desk, where the staff take over at once. Their face fills with relief at the sight. Someone brings water and a chair and a kind word. 'Thank you,' they keep saying to you, over and over. But your own room is waiting across the hall, and you can't stay long.

text.A2: You stop and look across the great hall. People stream past under the high glass roof, all in a hurry, all alone. Everyone is going somewhere. Only one figure stands still, far off, watching. Something about them stops your breath.
text.B1: You stop and look across the great hall. People stream past under the high glass roof, all in a hurry, all alone. Everyone is going somewhere today. Only one figure stands still, far off, watching. Something about them stops your breath.
text.B2: You stop and look out across the great hall. People stream past under the high glass roof, all in a hurry, all alone with their day. Everyone is going somewhere, fast. Only one figure stands quite still, far off, watching the crowd. And something about them, something you can't name, stops your breath.

text.A2: The nerves turn as hard as they get now. Your chest is tight, your mouth is dry, your hands won't settle. It's hard to think, hard to breathe, hard to care. Your bag feels like lead. This is the worst of it.
text.B1: The nerves turn as hard as they get now. Your chest is tight, your mouth is dry, your hands won't settle. It's hard to think, hard to breathe, hard to care. Your bag feels like lead in your hand. This is the worst of it — the hardest part of the whole day.
text.B2: The nerves turn as hard as they are going to get now. Your chest is tight, your mouth is dry, your hands won't settle at all. It's hard to think, hard to breathe, hard to care about any of it. Your bag feels like lead in your hand. This is the worst of it — the hardest part of the whole long day.

text.A2: Old Sam presses something into your hands — a good pen and a clean folder for your papers. 'For the room,' he says. 'Go on, take it. Walk in looking like you mean it.' His face is kind under the shop light. It's what he has to give today, and he gives it gladly.
text.B1: Old Sam presses something into your hands — a good pen and a clean folder for your papers. 'For the room,' he says. 'Go on, take it. Walk in looking like you mean it.' His face is kind under the shop light. It's what he has to give today, and he gives all of it gladly.
text.B2: Old Sam presses something into your hands — a good pen and a clean folder for your papers. 'For the room,' he says. 'Go on, take it. Walk in looking like you mean it.' His face is kind under the shop light. It's what he has to give today, and he gives every bit of it gladly.

text.A2: At the sign-in desk, people are pushing for the last forms and slots. Voices rise, elbows go, panic spreading fast down the line. One more shove and it's a row. You can try to calm them and sort it fairly. Or you can grab your slot and go.
text.B1: At the sign-in desk, people are pushing for the last forms and slots. Voices rise, elbows go, panic spreading fast down the line. One more shove and it's a row. You can try to calm them and sort it out fairly. Or you can grab your slot and go.
text.B2: At the sign-in desk, people are pushing and grabbing for the last forms and slots. Voices rise, elbows go, panic spreading fast down the whole line. One more shove and it tips into a row. You can try to calm them down and sort it out fairly. Or you can grab your own slot and go.

text.A2: A quiet corner off the main hall, where the noise falls away. You stop to breathe. Then you see her — by the lifts, half-turned, achingly familiar. Someone you knew once, and lost. Your heart goes still.
text.B1: A quiet corner off the main hall, where the noise falls away. You stop to breathe for a moment. Then you see her — by the lifts, half-turned, achingly familiar. Someone you knew once, and lost. Your heart goes still.
text.B2: A quiet corner off the main hall, where the noise falls away to almost nothing. You stop a moment just to breathe. Then you see her — standing by the lifts, half-turned, achingly familiar. Someone you knew once, and worked beside, and lost. And your heart goes quite still in your chest.

text.A2: Far across the hall, a figure stands where the crowd thins. They seem to be looking right at you — then away, then back. You can't place them, and yet you can. Something in you needs to know. And something in you is afraid to.
text.B1: Far across the hall, a figure stands where the crowd thins out. They seem to be looking right at you — then away, then back again. You can't place them, and yet you can. Something in you needs to know. And something in you is afraid to.
text.B2: Far across the hall, a figure stands where the crowd thins out. They seem to be looking right at you — then away, then back again, slowly. You can't quite place them, and yet somehow you can. Something in you needs to know who it is. And something in you, just as strong, is afraid to.

text.A2: You cross the hall toward them and lift a hand. They don't see you, or don't show it. Then you catch their face in the light — and the years fall away. You know that face. You know it far too well.
text.B1: You cross the hall toward them and lift a hand. They don't see you, or don't show it. Then you catch their face in the light — and the years fall away at once. You know that face. You know it far too well.
text.B2: You cross the hall toward them and lift a hand. They don't see you, or don't choose to show it. Then you catch their face in the light — and all the years fall away at once. You know that face. You know it far, far too well. And your legs carry you on toward it anyway.

text.A2: You reach her, and your heart turns over. It's Maya — older now, the same steady eyes, a lanyard round her neck. She's on the panel. The one you fell out with, years ago, and never put right. No time to think. You have to speak now.
text.B1: You reach her, and your heart turns over. It's Maya — older now, the same steady eyes, a lanyard round her neck. She's on the panel. The one you fell out with, years ago, and never put right. There's no time to think. You have to say something now.
text.B2: You reach her, and your heart turns right over. It's Maya — older now, the same steady eyes, a staff lanyard round her neck. She's on the panel. The one you fell out with, years ago, and never once put right. There's no time to stop and think. You have to say something, and say it now.

text.A2: You call her name across the hall, and for a moment there's nothing. Then she turns, and her face changes — surprise, then something softer, harder to read. 'It's you,' she says. And you hear how much is in those two words.
text.B1: You call her name across the hall, and for a moment there's nothing at all. Then she turns, and her face changes — surprise, then something softer, harder to read. 'It's you,' she says. And you can hear how much is in those two words.
text.B2: You call her name across the hall, and for a long moment there's nothing at all. Then she turns, and her whole face changes — surprise first, then something softer, and much harder to read. 'It's you,' she says, quietly. And you can hear just how much is packed into those two small words.

text.A2: You face Maya at last, and the years come up between you. Slowly, the hard set of her shoulders eases. She grips your arm. 'So it's you, in there,' she says quietly. 'After all this time.' Even now, she's thinking of the door you both closed.
text.B1: You face Maya at last, and all the years come up between you. Slowly, the hard set of her shoulders eases. She grips your arm. 'So it's you, in there,' she says quietly. 'After all this time.' Even now, she's thinking of the door you both closed.
text.B2: You face Maya at last, and all the years come up between you at once. Slowly, the hard set of her shoulders eases a little. She grips your arm. 'So it's you, in there,' she says quietly. 'After all this time.' Even now, standing here, she's thinking of the door the two of you closed. You keep your eyes on hers, and you don't look away.

text.A2: You turn to slip away — then stop short. There's no avoiding it, not now, not today. Not her on the panel and you at the door. It's face it or lose it, and she knows it too. Her eyes follow you across the hall.
text.B1: You turn to slip away — then stop short. There's no avoiding it, not now, not today. Not with her on the panel and you at the door. It's face it or lose it now, and she knows it too. Her eyes follow you across the hall.
text.B2: You turn to slip away — then stop short. There's no avoiding it, not now, not today of all days. Not with her on the panel and you about to walk in. It's face it or lose the whole thing now, and she knows it too. Her eyes follow you across the hall, steady and sad.

text.A2: Maya looks at you, her eyes clearer now. 'We were a team once,' she says. 'Then it all went wrong, and neither of us called. My fault as much as yours. It's a long, sad story.' And you hear just how long it is.
text.B1: Maya looks at you, her eyes clearer now. 'We were a team once,' she says. 'Then it all went wrong, and neither of us called. My fault as much as yours. It's a long, sad story.' And you can hear just how long it is.
text.B2: Maya looks at you, her eyes a little clearer now. 'We were a team once, you and me,' she says. 'Then it all went wrong, and neither of us ever called. My fault as much as yours. It's a long, sad story.' And you can hear, in her voice, just how long it is.

text.A2: You decide to clear the air before you walk in. You and Maya, after all these years apart. It's a small thing, next to everything else today. But it's not nothing. Some shut doors can still be opened.

text.B2: You decide to clear the air before you walk in there. You and Maya, after all these long years apart. It's a small thing, perhaps, next to everything else today. But it is not nothing. Some shut doors can still be opened, if someone tries. And tonight, it seems, that someone is you.

text.A2: To the room, with that said.
text.B1: To the room, with that said.
text.B2: To the room, with that said.

text.A2: The figure stands still, and your nerve works at you, slow and cruel. And yet you came all this way, through all of it, to this. You can't just walk past and pretend. You have to go closer and be sure who it is.
text.B1: The figure stands still, and your nerve works at you, slow and cruel. And yet you came all this way, through all of it, to this moment. You can't just walk past and pretend. You have to go closer and be sure who it is.
text.B2: The figure stands quite still, and your nerve works away at you, slow and cruel. And yet you came all this way, through all of it, to this very moment. You can't just walk past and pretend you didn't see. You have to go closer and be sure who it is.

text.A2: You go closer, and you know her at once. It's Maya — your old partner, not seen in years, not since the day it all fell apart. Then she turns and sees you too. There's no hiding now.
text.B1: You go closer, and you know her at once. It's Maya — your old partner, not seen in years, not since the day it all fell apart. Then she turns and sees you too. There's no hiding from it now.
text.B2: You go closer still, and you know her at once. It's Maya — your old partner, not seen in years, not since the day it all fell so badly apart. Then she turns and sees you too, and her eyes widen. There's no hiding from it now, for either of you.

text.A2: Reese turns up one last time, folder in hand. 'Still doing it the hard way?' he says. 'Give it up. Let me sort you out — last chance to take the easy road, friend.' The same easy smile. The same old lie.
